title: Short Stuff: Kentucky Meat Shower
summary: Short Stuff episode on the Kentucky Meat Shower of March 3, 1876, when meat-like chunks fell from a clear sky onto Rebecca Crouch's farm in Kentucky. The hosts cover the witnesses (Crouch, her grandson Alan, neighbor Harrison Gill, butcher Frizz Frisbee, neighbor Eli Willis), the failed theories (rehydrated frog spawn, cyanobacteria proposed by Leopold Brandis), the vulture vomiting explanation proposed by Dr. L.D. Cast and Bind in the Louisville Medical News, and art professor Kurt Goda's later jelly bean project. The episode was suggested by listener Ben Fisher.

segments.title: Opening banter and listener suggestion
segments.summary: Hosts introduce the Short Stuff episode, joke about the title sounding like a band name, and credit listener Ben Fisher for suggesting the topic. They note they had not heard of the event.

segments.title: The March 1876 meat fall on Rebecca Crouch's farm
segments.summary: On March 3, 1876, Rebecca Crouch and grandson Alan were making soap outside when chunks of meat fell from a clear sky over roughly a football field. Pieces were palm-sized or smaller. Neighbor Harrison Gill verified the meat next day, finding it stuck to fences and briars.

segments.title: Butcher's taste test and neighbor Eli Willis
segments.summary: Local butcher Frizz Frisbee tasted a sample, found it milky and watery, and spit it out. Other people described it as brown and similar in look to veal or mutton but foul-smelling. Neighbor Eli Willis took some home to cook, and his family stopped him and threw it away.

segments.title: Sponsor break
segments.summary: Mid-episode break before the discussion of samples and theories.

segments.title: Samples and early theories: frog spawn and cyanobacteria
segments.summary: Samples were sent to Transylvania University and other places. Theories included rehydrated frog spawn, which the hosts say fails because it was not raining, and cyanobacteria proposed by water sanitation expert Leopold Brandis, who called it star jelly-like low vegetable life.

segments.title: Vulture vomit explanation
segments.summary: Chemistry professor Dr. L.D. Cast and Bind proposed in 1876, in the Louisville Medical News, that it was mass vulture vomiting. Vultures vomit to lighten weight or as defense, and they eat decomposing animals.

segments.title: Kurt Goda's objection and vultures at altitude
segments.summary: Art professor Kurt Goda argued for decades that Crouch would have seen vultures overhead. The hosts respond that vultures can fly up to about 20,000 feet, so a flock could have vomited unseen onto the farm.

segments.title: Kentucky meat shower jelly beans
segments.summary: Goda later had the flavor compounds made into Kentucky meat shower jelly beans, handed out at a state fair and the Court Days Festival. Tasters compared them to bacon, lamb going rotten, and strawberry pork chops. Goda told Atlas Obscura he finds them vile.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts close the episode, with a hope that Professor Goda will hear how they did, and give the standard iHeartRadio production credit.
